source: Battambang Provincial Department of Agriculture and the Cambodia Northwest Provinces Fruit Culture Development Committee (financial support from the SEILA Programme), Khmer translation of Photpeechon Whayooathdee, "ដំណាំខ្នុរ (Jackfruit)", "Translation Copy No. 4", January 1997 (500 copies printed). This is a Khmer translation of a Thai-language original: Whayooathdee, Photpeechon, "Jackfruit (2nd edition)", Nonthaburi Province, Thailand: Agriculture Lover's Printing House, 1988. Cover illustration source: Forestry/Fuelwood Research and Development Project, 1992, "Growing Multipurpose Trees on Small Farms", Winrock International, Bangkok. Other artwork by Sarath, Som, Center for Social Development, Phnom Penh, Dec. 1996.
text:
This chapter discusses techniques growers use to spread jackfruit fruiting and harvest over a longer period of the year rather than having all fruit ripen in a single short season, which the text presents as valuable both for smoothing household consumption and for capturing better market prices by avoiding the general market glut that occurs at peak season. Approaches discussed include managing flowering timing on different branches or different trees (through pruning timing, selective fruit thinning, and fertilization timing) so that not all fruit set and mature simultaneously, and maintaining a mix of early-, mid-, and late-fruiting named varieties within the same planting so that harvest is naturally staggered across the year.

The chapter also gives guidance on estimating and tracking fruit maturity so that harvest timing decisions (letting some fruit mature later, picking others earlier) can be made deliberately rather than by default, including visual and other cues used to judge how close a given fruit is to full ripeness (covered in more depth in the following harvesting chapter).

Pests and insect damage: this chapter also includes a substantial pest-focused section covering insect threats that can affect fruit quality and marketability, most importantly:
- Fruit fly (the text names the fruit fly as Bactrocera umbrosa Fabr., also discussing Bactrocera dorsalis with an illustrated life-cycle diagram of egg, larva/maggot, pupa, and adult fly stages). The text describes the fly laying eggs in developing fruit, the larvae feeding inside and causing the fruit to rot and drop prematurely, and describes the insect's approximate life-cycle length (on the order of about three weeks) and damage patterns, citing entomological references (Ahmad Yunus and A. Balasubramaniam's work on major crop pests in Peninsular Malaysia, and a citation to the Philippine Journal of Agriculture) reproduced by the translators as background sources.
- Mealybugs/scale insects ("សអ្វព្រកសែសម្កែសសិ" / scale-insect section) and ants: the chapter discusses sap-sucking pests found on fruit and young shoots, their association with ants that farm them for honeydew, and general control measures such as physical removal, encouraging natural predators, and targeted treatment of heavily infested fruit or shoots, along with orchard sanitation (removing fallen, infested fruit promptly) to reduce pest carryover between seasons.
- Termites: the chapter also references termite ("ស្រមោច") damage risk to weakened trees and standing dead wood near the tree base, recommending sanitation and prompt treatment when activity is found (overlapping with guidance given in the home-garden chapter).

The chapter frames pest management as directly connected to the goal of extending the marketable harvest window, since fruit damaged by fruit fly or heavy scale-insect infestation cannot be held for later, staggered sale and must be used or discarded immediately.
